content:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to give the court 30 days' notice before making any proposals to alter existing construction plans at the Kennedy Center, including "demolition."

The order largely reaffirms the terms of a previous injunction blocking the government from closing or altering the building. It comes as officials work to close and potentially even destroy the presidential memorial and performing arts centre, after a court ruled that President Trump's name must be removed from the building.

The president told reporters on Wednesday that the building could be "torn down" if his name could not be added back on in some form.

Later on Wednesday night, Trump was photographed aboard Air Force One looking at an image that appeared to show the Kennedy Centre being torn down, with the words "KENNEDY CENTER DEMOLISHED" displayed on it.

The text was partially obscured but could be seen faintly through the plane's window. Trump appeared at a separate window nearby, looking at the sign.

In his Thursday order, Judge Charles Cooper granted the plaintiff and Kennedy Centre trustee, Ohio Democratic Representative Joyce Beatty, permission to collect evidence regarding the photograph of Trump looking at the image.

The Ohio Democrat has been leading the fight against his takeover of the storied arts institution and the "unlawful" closure of the memorial honouring former President John F. Kennedy.

A Kennedy Centre board made up of appointees handpicked by Trump voted on Tuesday to close the centre for up to two years for a US$257 million renovation.

Beatty asked the judge for an emergency hearing after the closure was announced and submitted additional legal filings on Thursday after the photograph surfaced.

The latest filing said: "A photograph circulating on social media shows President Trump on Air Force One looking at a placard that appears to read 'Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.'" The filing also included an enlarged version of the image.

Beatty's lawyers said in their court filing that the board's closure of the Kennedy Centre was "a transparent pretext to justify permanently shuttering the centre. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning."

They asked the judge to make "perfectly clear" that his previous order "prohibits the demolition of the building."

Kennedy Centre executive director and chief operating officer Matt Floehr said in a filing of his own on Thursday that the temporary closure was due to "ongoing structural deterioration caused by the building's age that poses a serious risk to public safety."

The centre, established by Congress and opened in 1971, is no longer open to the public during regular business hours.
